doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

title: GI Bill school and his refusal to learn to read music
summary: Ware passes the GI Bill music test, attends one lesson a week, but fears reading will cost him his natural ear, as the story of Burt Brazier convinced him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I went to teach him -- this is when I got myself

kind of messed up, but I wanted to make some money -- not make some money, but go to school on the GI Bill, I had that option, and I went down and I took the test. I passed. The lady seemed to be surprised that I passed the test. She said, 'Well, you passed every one of them' -- you know. But hey, I had been hearing sounds all my life.

Yeah, a music test, you know. Is this note a flat or is that a sharp? You know? Well, I say, well, I want to study bass. Now I was afraid to learn how to read music, simply because I had a mental block about it. I'll go back some years when I was working down there at that club on 31st -- the Tuxedo Inn -- working with Buster Bennett and his band.

Martha Davis, yeah. An alto player came through there out of St. Louis named Burt Brazier. Now Burt come through Chicago with a pianist -- only had one leg, Greer? and a drummer was named Sonny Greer; they were all out of St. Louis. Swinging little cats. And I mean they were older than I was. I was just, like I said, just a teenager. And they were playing, oh, to me -- Burt was sounding like Benny Carter would sound, you know, on alto. But he didn't know the music. I didn't find this out until later, because I had run in to him up in Grand Rapids, Michigan when I joined

the WPA band -- he was in the WPA band. He remembered me. And I said, 'Burt?' And he said, 'Bubble ...' -- he used to call everybody 'Bubble Kitchen'. He said, 'Bubble Kitchen, I never learned how to read music. I can hardly play it unless it's written out.' And I took that advice and I figured if I learned how to read, I would lose all my natural ability.

That was just ignorance on my part, you know. But through the years, I was afraid, you know. I could play -- anything I hear I could play, and I can anticipate. It's funny, but I've always been able to do that. I made recordings with people -- spontaneous. We'd play and I know exactly what he's gonna do, you know.

And to me, that's a gift. And maybe I was lazy, which I guess, I was. I went to school -- my father was teaching there in downtown Chicago -- and I went down on the GI Bill -- I only had to go one hour a week, and you know, I couldn't even make that? And he thought I was phenomenal -- he said, 'How could you play so when you never studied?' And I mean, he liked me; he would have helped me tremendously, but I had hooked up in to something else, which was against everything, so I stopped going. And I figure that everything I've done through the years has been for the best, or that it was the way it was supposed to be.
